analysis.one_liner: Restores student borrowers' bankruptcy rights and stops Social Security, tax-refund, and wage garnishment collection.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees in July 2017, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy like almost any other debt, end collection through Social Security offsets, tax-refund seizures, and wage garnishment, and reinstate a six-year time limit on lawsuits over student loans. It would also let parents with PLUS loans into income-based repayment, forgive half the balance of direct loans for borrowers who work five years in public service and make 60 payments, bar loan default from being used to suspend professional licenses, and stop colleges from withholding transcripts over default. It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 44 million student loan borrowers, especially the millions in default or long-term hardship: they could escape crushing debt through bankruptcy, keep their retirement and Social Security income, their paychecks, and their tax refunds, and keep access to transcripts and licenses needed to work. Parents with PLUS loans would gain income-based repayment options, and public-service workers would get loan forgiveness after five years instead of ten.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student borrowers, especially those in default

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the special rule in bankruptcy law that makes student loans nearly impossible to discharge, putting them back on the same footing as most other consumer debt [S3].
Prohibits collecting federal student debt by offsetting Social Security, railroad retirement, or black lung benefits, seizing federal tax refunds, or garnishing wages [S2].
Reinstates a six-year statute of limitations on lawsuits to collect student loans, which federal law had eliminated [S3].
Excludes discharged student loan debt from taxable income, so borrowers are not hit with a tax bill on forgiven debt, and allows 529 college-savings funds to pay down student loans [S2].
Opens income-based repayment to parents with PLUS loans on behalf of dependent students, who are currently excluded [S2].
Requires the Education Department to cancel 50% of interest and principal on direct loans for borrowers who work in public service jobs for five years and make 60 monthly payments [S2].
Bars evidence of loan default from being used in proceedings over a professional or vocational license, and prohibits colleges from withholding transcripts because a former student defaulted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the federal loan program, because debts discharged in bankruptcy or forgiven under the public-service provision are not repaid; lenders and guaranty agencies lose their bankruptcy-proof status; and the collection industry loses garnishment, refund-offset, and benefit-offset work. Colleges could no longer use transcript holds as a collection lever.

drawbacks.text: The bankruptcy provision is broad: it applies to all educational loans with no income test or waiting period, so some high earners could walk away from loans others paid for, at taxpayer cost [S3].

The five-year, 50%-cancellation public-service provision would forgive loans after only 60 payments, a faster and costlier write-off than the existing ten-year, 120-payment program, and would apply to loans borrowed before the law took effect [S3].
Making loans dischargeable would likely raise the cost or restrict availability of private student lending, since lenders would price in bankruptcy risk [S3].
The bill was introduced with no cosponsors and no companion Senate bill, so it never had a realistic path even if a committee had acted [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are genuinely strong and would have made a real difference for millions of borrowers in default, ending punitive collection from retirement checks and paychecks and restoring a bankruptcy safety net. The cost is real too: taxpayer losses from broader discharge and faster forgiveness, and the bill's lack of any cosponsors or committee attention suggests its drafting had little buy-in even from its own party. On balance it was a substantial if expensive package of borrower protections that received no serious consideration.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever scheduled a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson of Florida introduced the bill on July 28, 2017 [S1].
It was referred simultaneously to the Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Oversight and Government Reform committees [S5].
No committee ever reported it, no hearing or markup is recorded, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill never gained a single cosponsor in the House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student-loan collection channels and the federal loan program are unaffected; borrowers in default remain subject to garnishment, refund offsets, and transcript holds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student-debt collectors and the federal loan program

for.name: Rep. Frederica Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Student Loan Borrowers' Bill of Rights Act of 2017 on July 28, 2017.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Oversight and Government Reform Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral.

against.name: House leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration in two and a half years.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no House Republican ever signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: The bill strips their most powerful collection tools: wage garnishment, tax-refund seizure, and Social Security offsets, plus a six-year time limit on collection lawsuits. Servicers' revenue depends on aggressive collection of defaulted federal loans.

industries.industry: Guaranty agencies and private student lenders
industries.note: Making all educational loans dischargeable in bankruptcy removes the special protection that makes student debt uniquely safe to lend against, and the six-year statute of limitations limits how long agencies can pursue defaulters.
Most of the bill helps their students and borrowers, but it bans transcript and degree holds for defaulters, a lever many institutions use to pressure former students into paying.

Bankruptcy discharges, faster public-service cancellation, and blocked collection channels mean more unpaid balances borne by the federal government, i.e., taxpayers. The trade buys protections for struggling borrowers.
